work_order.understanding:
QA failed PR #59 (issue #55) on two bugs, both in test/web/pages.test.js, both introduced by this PR, both reproducible. I reproduced every one of them myself on 97f97bb rather than taking the report's numbers: the clean tree is 485 pass / 0 fail; a coordinated rename of '.page-title' to '.pageHeading' across src/web/styles.css and src/web/pages.js gives exactly one failure, 'BUG-7: a pseudo-class is decided, not stripped'; appending '#main h1 { line-height: 1.25; }' to the shipped sheet gives one failure, in the test 'nothing in the shipped stylesheet beats the class rule for the page h1'; ':root { all: revert; }' gives one failure in the same test; and ':root { font: revert; }' gives four, including the guard itself. I also ran the four neighbouring spellings the report lists but does not enumerate — 'h1[data-testid] { font-size: 1.4rem; }', '#main h1 { margin: 0; }', '#main h1 { font-size: 1.4rem !important; }', '#main h1 { margin-block-start: 0; }' — and each gives exactly that one failure, which is what tells me the cause is one thing and not four.

WAS THE v3 DIAGNOSIS WRONG? No, and I want to be exact about that, because 'the plan was wrong' is not the finding here and saying it would send the implementer looking for a different theory. v3's root_cause said the guard's contract is a property of the whole pipeline and not of the sites, and both of these bugs are exactly what that sentence predicts. What v3 did was write each new rule at the places it happened to be thinking about. The value rule — 'a report is about a VALUE, so a rule that restates the held value is silent, and revert is a removal rather than a set' — went into outrankingPageTitleDeclarations and its two messages, and did not go into the second place in the same file that answers the identical question: the shipped-stylesheet probe, which reads the whole sheet by hand and filters on 'reaches the h1' and 'outranks' and stops there. And the 'pin it to the resolved class' rule, which v3 stated and which AC-3 certifies, was applied to the guard's callers and not to the cascade contract's own fixtures, four of which spell the class out.

So the diagnosis is right and the enforcement was partial. The change from this attempt is not a new theory of the bug; it is that the property is asserted over the SET of places that answer the question rather than at the places an author was looking at, and that the set membership is itself checked by a test. Otherwise this issue finds a fifth place.

THIS IS NOT THE 'CRITERION IS WRONG' CASE, again. The rollup marks exactly AC-3 and AC-18 as failed, and those two criteria are the ones these two bugs violate; both still read correctly and neither is touched. AC-1 to AC-19 carry forward byte-for-byte, none renumbered and none dropped. On a fourth pass the temptation is to soften AC-18 — it is the restatement criterion, and the failing behaviour looks at first like 'the criterion is too strict' — and here that would be wrong: a criterion edited to match a false alarm is the artefact this pipeline can least afford, because every future QA run would then certify the defect.

NOTHING HERE IS A DEFECT IN THE SHIPPED APP. src/web/pages.js:57 and src/web/styles.css:137 are correct as shipped, this change touches neither, and the browser reads 22.4px / 28px / 0px on the clean tree across all 25 shells.
work_order.root_cause:
One sentence, and both bugs are the two instances of it: in this file a decision is repeatedly pinned to a literal instead of to the thing the decision is about, and each pin is invisible because a literal that stops matching is quiet rather than loud.

1. THE FIXTURES PIN THE CLASS TO A LITERAL. The cascade contract builds every case through `cls` — the class read off the rendered h1, which is the convention the whole guard is built on and the thing AC-3 certifies. Four cases do not. test/web/pages.test.js:3708 ('@layer base { .page-title { font-size: 2.4rem; } }'), :3813 ('.page-title::after { font-size: 2.4rem; }'), :3814 ('.page-title[data-x] { font-size: 2.4rem; }') and :3895 ('h1:is(.page-title) { font-size: 2.4rem; }'). The last is the red one: after a coordinated rename the h1 carries 'pageHeading', the selector matches nothing, branchReaches proves it out, the guard returns [] where the case demands a report, and the suite goes red on a stylesheet that is correct. The other three are worse, and they are why this is a major rather than a nuisance: each is a QUIET case, and a selector that matches nothing is quiet too. After a rename they keep passing while testing nothing at all — 'page-title::after' no longer has anything to do with a pseudo-element or with the class, it is a selector for a class nothing carries, and the suite cannot tell the two apart. That is the false-pass direction, and it is silent by construction rather than by accident. This is not a new shape: the same report from the round before filed the same species against the 25-shell count assertion, and v3 answered it with a second anchor at :1630. The recurrence says the anchor was placed rather than the convention enforced.

2. THE SHIPPED-SHEET PROBE RE-IMPLEMENTS THE CASCADE AND DOES NOT INHERIT THE VALUE DECISION. outrankingPageTitleDeclarations decides a report in four steps: reach the h1, outrank the class rule, and then the two the last change added — does the declaration the cascade KEEPS put the group at a value the h1 is not already at (restates), and, on the root, is it a removal rather than a set. The probe at test/web/pages.test.js:3112-3139 asks only the first two, and its root-side assertion at :3153-3160 asks whether a root-reaching branch declares font-size, font or 'all' as a bare property name, with no regard for the value. The two are answering different questions and the probe is the stricter of the pair, so every rule the guard has already decided is a no-op is still a 'violation' to the probe. Its failure messages name a selector and say nothing about a value, which is the self-refuting message the last change was filed to remove, arriving through the other door. This is not a new shape either: it is v3's own root_cause, 'the one-directional property is a property of the pipeline and not of the matcher', restated one level up, in a probe rather than in a matcher.

3. THE 'revert' EXEMPTION IS A SPELLING RATHER THAN A RULE. At test/web/pages.test.js:3020 it is written `carried.property === 'all' && declarationText(carried) === 'all: revert'` — one property, one exact value. 'revert' is a removal; ':root { font: revert }' is the same removal in another property, and the guard reports it with a message asserting as fact that the h1's font-size 'moves with it, away from font-size: 1.4rem' while the declared value is 'revert' and the browser reads 22.4px. A guard that exempts one spelling of a concept is a guard that will report the next spelling, and this one has already reported three of them. Note the asymmetry that must survive the fix, because getting it wrong is a false pass rather than a false alarm: on the ROOT, 'revert' cannot move anything the class rule's rem is measured against, because the shipped root is already at the user-agent default; on the H1, 'revert' drops the class rule's own declaration and the user-agent's 'h1 { font-size: 2em }' takes over, so '#main h1 { all: revert }' genuinely does move the heading and must stay reported. The exemption is a fact about where the declaration applies, and nothing in the file says so.

Underneath all three is the thing v3 stated and then applied by enumeration: the file has a contract, and a contract stated as a list of sites is a list of sites. 'A step may SKIP a rule only on a proof, may REPORT a rule it cannot decide about, and may never manufacture a proof it did not decode' is true of the reader, the tokenizer, the matcher and the value comparison — and equally true of the probe, which is a fifth step and was not in the list. Same for 'the class is read off the element, never hard-coded' and the four fixtures that are. The fix that holds is the one that makes each of these an invariant over the set of places that answer the question, with the set itself pinned by a test, rather than the fifth addition to the list.
work_order.approach:
Test-only, confined to test/web/pages.test.js. The production files are correct and are not touched.

The difference from v3 is structural and worth stating before the steps, because it is the whole answer to 'why did the last attempt, whose diagnosis was right, still fail'. v3 wrote each rule at the sites it was thinking about. This writes each rule ONCE, in a function every place that answers the question calls, and adds a test that fails if a place stops calling it. Three invariants, three mechanisms.

1 — THE CLASS IS THE RESOLVED ELEMENT, IN EVERY FIXTURE, AND THE RULE IS CHECKED. Interpolate the four sites (:3708, :3813, :3814, :3895) through `cls`, the way the twenty other class-coupled cases in the contract already do. That is the red half of BUG-9 and it is one character each.

The quiet half cannot be fixed by editing four strings, because nothing about a quiet case is observable from outside: a fixture hardcoded to '.page-title' and a fixture interpolated from `cls` produce identical verdicts today, because `cls` IS 'page-title' today. There is no behavioural formulation of the check, so the check has to be a source audit, and this file already has the idiom — the pinning test at :1609 reads its own source and anchors on an unsplittable needle. Do the same here, with one addition that makes it decidable: the class literals that are CORRECT are the two vocabulary tables, where the case is about what a class selector is worth in the cascade rather than about the shipped class — specificityOf('.page-title') is [0,1,0] at :4091, ':is(#a, h1.page-title)' is [1,0,0] at :4113, and the reachability table at :4162 ('.page-title-extra' is not the class, '.page-title::after' does not reach the element). Hoist those into two named constants, CLASS_VOCABULARY and REACH_VOCABULARY, with a comment saying why they do not follow a rename, and have the audit require that every remaining class literal in the file is either inside one of those two constants or is prose in an assertion message. A fifth literal is then red on its own, before it is ever wrong.

Then the second half of AC-20, in-suite: a case that performs the coordinated rename in memory — the way :3375 already does — and re-runs the class-coupled fixtures against the renamed chain, asserting that 'h1:is(.pageHeading)' is still reported and that '.pageHeading::after' is still silent for the reason it is silent rather than for the reason a selector matching nothing is silent. A hardcoded fixture fails the first of those; the second is what the audit above is for, and both are needed because they fail in opposite directions.

2 — ONE VALUE DECISION, CALLED BY EVERY PLACE THAT ANSWERS THE QUESTION. Extract the composition that outrankingPageTitleDeclarations currently performs inline at :2940 (restates) and :3020 (the revert exemption) into one function, and have BOTH its push points and BOTH of the probe's filters call it:

  movesTheHeldValue(declaration, group, subject)

subject is 'h1' or 'root', and it is a parameter rather than an implicit difference between callers on purpose: the revert exemption is true for one subject and false for the other, and the reason is a fact about where the declaration applies, so it belongs in the one function with the reason written next to it. False when the declaration is null; false when subject is 'root' and the declaration is a removal; false when `restates` says the group is already at that value; true otherwise. The shorthand rule stays where it is, inside `restates`, because it is already correct there and moving it would only be churn.

`isRemoval(declaration)` is the value, importance stripped and trimmed, equal to 'revert' case-insensitively. Exactly that: 'revert-layer', 'unset', 'initial' and 'inherit' are not removals and are not exempted, and the test that says so is the one that keeps the word from being the rule.

3 — THE PROBE STOPS BEING A SECOND CASCADE. It stays — its claim is the strongest one in the file, an exhaustive structural read of the whole shipped sheet rather than a spot check, and it is what makes the first assertion of the test non-vacuous. What changes is that it now asks the same question, which means two concrete changes and neither is a filter tweak:

  (a) It stops filtering on 'the rule declares a guarded property somewhere' and starts asking which declaration the cascade KEEPS for each group, with the same `cascadingWinner` helper the guard uses (:1969). That is the structural reason the probe could not simply have been given a restates filter: it never picked a winner, so there was no declaration to ask about. '#main h1 { margin: 0; margin-top: 24px }' keeps the longhand and is still reported, and the probe has to reach the same verdict for the same reason.
  (b) Its h1-side assertion is restated to the claim it can actually support — 'no rule but the class rule may reach the h1, outrank it, and put a group at a value the h1 is not already at' — and its root-side assertion replaces the bare `entry.property === 'all'` test with `movesTheHeldValue(entry, 'font-size', 'root')`, so ':root { all: revert }' and ':root { font: revert }' are silent on both sides.

4 — PIN IT BOTH WAYS, AND PIN THE PINNER. The cross-check QA asked for: a table in which each entry carries the verdict the guard must return AND the verdict the probe must return for the same appended rule, and the two must agree — silent together or reporting together. The table carries the thirteen no-op spellings from AC-21 and two real overrides ('#main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; }', '#main h1 { line-height: 2; }') so the green half cannot be bought by deleting the probe. This is the assertion that makes 'they cannot drift again' a fact rather than a hope, and it is the one entry in this order that would still be red if somebody later loosened only one of the two.

5 — THE ASYMMETRY IS PINNED FROM BOTH SIDES, so the exemption cannot be generalised. '#main h1 { all: revert; }' stays REPORTED and ':root { font: revert; }' becomes silent, with the reason for each written next to the case: on the root a removal can only carry the rem back toward the default the shipped root is already at; on the h1 it drops the class rule's own declaration and hands the element to the user-agent's 'h1 { font-size: 2em }', which is 32px on a 16px root. Silencing the h1 side would be a false pass, and it is the mistake a reader of the code would most plausibly make next.

6 — KEEP WHAT WAS ALREADY RIGHT. The element chain resolved from the rendered markup, the quote- and bracket-aware scanner, the layer-rank ordering with its !important inversion, the escape decoder, the reachability function and the two predicates now under it, the value cross-check and the shorthand rule inside it, the @media/@supports condition naming, the message wording, the pinning tests at :1609 and the 25-shell count anchor, and the class-to-rule link that makes a coordinated rename green at all. Do not re-derive them; re-run them. The 485 cases on the clean tree are the regression suite for v3's work and this change must not disturb a single one of them.

risks: The temptation this order exists to resist is the quiet one. Every fix below makes MORE things green, and the only thing that tells a correct widening from a false pass is the browser control. Each added exemption must arrive with its measured control in the same commit, and an exemption whose control was not measured is not finished. If the implementer cannot measure one, stop and say so rather than shipping the exemption.

The h1-side asymmetry in §5 is the sharpest edge here. Getting the revert exemption wrong in the permissive direction turns '#main h1 { all: revert; }' from a true report into a false pass, and the suite goes green on a stylesheet that genuinely moves the heading. It is pinned as a test, and the pin is the thing to check first if anything in §2-§4 goes wrong.

The source audit for class literals can be made brittle in both directions. Too strict and it demands a rename-proof rewrite of the two vocabulary tables, which are correct as literals and would lose their meaning. Too loose and it accepts a fifth fixture. The allow-list must be the two named constants and nothing else; a per-line allow-list of literals would re-create the problem it is fixing.

The probe must keep reading the whole shipped sheet by hand. Sharing the value decision with the guard does not make the probe redundant — its claim is exhaustive where the guard's is a verdict, and it is the assertion that would notice a guard that quietly stopped asking about half the sheet. The risk is the opposite mistake: deleting the probe because the guard now agrees with it, which is what AC-21's red half is there to catch.

The whole guard is still a test helper that makes a claim about CSS, which is the failure mode issue #55 was filed for. What this change does is narrow the class of defect — every answering place now calls one function — but a change to the reader, the tokenizer or the matcher can still introduce a defect this contract does not name. That is a standing property of the approach, not something this order removes.

.sdlc/memory/patterns/ is empty and this is the THIRD instance of one shape: a decision pinned to a literal instead of to the thing it decides about, turning a rename or a value into a silent pass in one direction and a false alarm in the other, in a guard whose own stated contract already forbade it. The first was the 25-shell count assertion, the second was the four fixtures, and the probe is the same shape a level up. The Librarian's write-up is owed and the entry should be about enforcement-over-a-set rather than about any one site.

A fourth attempt at the same shape. If the implementer believes the contract itself is wrong, that is a route request, not a quiet rewrite.

Modelling the user-agent default font-size, or resolving units so that 'font-size: 22.4px' is recognised as a restatement of 'font-size: 1.4rem'. Both are in residual_risks and both are the work of a different ticket; this change neither adds nor removes them.

A ':root { all: revert }' exemption being made sound in general. It is sound for the shipped sheet, where the root is already at the user-agent default, and unsound for a sheet that sets the root and then reverts it. Modelling that needs the UA default, which is out of scope above. The limitation is written into AC-22's control rather than left for the next reader.

Making the cascade check a rendered-value check in CI, turning the resolver into a shared CSS library or a src/ module, selector lists in @import'ed sheets, and recording anything in .sdlc/memory/**.
